Given your setup—Amex Gold (Dining/Groceries), Chase Sapphire Preferred (Travel), and USAA (Gas)—you have the "big" categories covered.

However, "random projects and hobbies" (like your electronics, beekeeping, or general DIY supplies) usually fall into "non-category" spend, meaning you are likely only earning 1x point/1% back on them right now.

Assuming you meant cards (not cars!), here are the best options to fill that gap based on your profile as a contractor and hobbyist.

1. The "Contractor" Play: American Express Blue Business Plus

Since you engage in contract work as a software engineer, you likely qualify for a business card (using your name as the sole proprietor). This is often the "missing link" for Amex users.

  • Why it fits you: It earns 2x Membership Rewards points on EVERYTHING (up to $50k/year).
  • The Strategy: It pairs perfectly with your Amex Gold. You earn the exact same points currency, but now you get 2x on all your "random" project runs—hardware stores, lumber, electronics parts—where you were previously getting 1x.
  • Annual Fee: $0.

2. The "Online Shopper" Play: Bank of America Customized Cash Rewards

If you buy most of your project gear online (e.g., Adafruit, eBay for Mindstorms, Amazon), this card is a powerhouse.

  • Why it fits you: You can choose your 3% category, and one option is "Online Shopping."
  • The Strategy: Set it to "Online Shopping" and use it exclusively for your digital purchases. It has a broad definition of "online" that covers almost any retailer with a website.
  • Annual Fee: $0.

3. The "Catch-All" Play: Citi Double Cash or Wells Fargo Active Cash

If your project spending is a mix of in-person (Home Depot, Lowes) and online, and you just want simplicity without worrying about business eligibility.

  • Why it fits you: These cards offer a flat 2% cash back on every single purchase.
  • The Strategy: Use this for anything that isn't Food, Travel, or Gas. It instantly doubles your return on those "random" expenses compared to your current setup.
  • Annual Fee: $0.

Summary Recommendation

  • If you want to earn more Travel Points: Go for the Amex Blue Business Plus. It keeps all your points in one bucket (Amex) and doubles your earning on projects.
  • If you want Cash Back: Go for the Bank of America Customized Cash if your spending is mostly online, or a 2% Flat Card if it's mixed.

turns.prompt_text: Do not most cards give a flat 2% cash back? What is the incentive for going with the business plan card? Especially with the high annual fees.
turns.response_html:
It is a common misconception that 2% is the standard; actually, most credit cards still offer only 1% to 1.5% on general purchases. Finding a card that offers a flat, unlimited 2% cash back (like the Citi Double Cash or Wells Fargo Active Cash) is considered "top tier" for a catch-all card, not the baseline.

Regarding your question about the business card—specifically the American Express Blue Business Plus—here is why it was recommended over a standard 2% cash back card, and why the "high fee" worry doesn't actually apply here:

1. It actually has NO Annual Fee

You mentioned high fees, and that is true for many business cards (like the Business Platinum), but the specific card recommended for you costs $0 per year. It is one of the rare powerful points cards that is completely free to hold.

2. The "Points vs. Cash" Math

This is the main incentive for you specifically, given that you already hold the Amex Gold.

  • Cash Back Card: If you spend $100 on your hobby supplies with a 2% card, you get $2. That’s it. The value is fixed.
  • Amex Blue Business Plus: If you spend that same $100, you get 2,000 Membership Rewards points.
    • If you redeem those points for statement credits, it's usually only 0.6 cents per point (bad value).
    • HOWEVER: Because you have the Amex Gold and Sapphire Preferred, you likely travel. If you transfer those points to an airline partner (like Delta, British Airways, or Air Canada), those 2,000 points can often be worth 3% or 4% in travel value.

The Strategy: By using this card, you are effectively earning "double points" that pool into the same account as your Gold card, helping you reach your next flight redemption much faster than if you split your earnings between Amex and a separate cash-back bank.

3. Eligibility is Easier Than You Think

You don't need an LLC or employees to get a business card. Since you mentioned "projects" and "hobbies"—if you ever sell a project, do freelance coding, or sell old electronics on eBay, you are considered a "sole proprietor" and can usually qualify using your own name and Social Security Number.

turns.prompt_text: Very nice, I do do freelance coding, how do I get on this?
turns.response_html:
That is excellent news—freelance coding is the "golden ticket" for business card eligibility. It makes you a legitimate Sole Proprietor in the eyes of the bank.

Since you are already in the American Express ecosystem (with the Gold and Blue), this process is often easier for you than for a new customer.

Here is exactly how to fill out the application to get the Blue Business Plus without needing a formal business entity like an LLC:

Step 1: The "Business Information" Section

This is the part that scares most people, but it’s actually very simple for a freelancer.

  • Legal Business Name: Put your First and Last Name.
    • Do not make up a business name (like "Austin's Coding") unless you have actually registered that name with the state.
  • Company Name on Card: This can be your name again, or you can get creative here if you want (e.g., "Austin Rognes Tech").
  • Business Address: Use your home address.
  • Company Structure: Select Sole Proprietorship.
  • Industry Type: Look for "Technology," "Professional Services," or "Computer/Data Processing."
  • Years in Business: Be honest. If you just started freelance coding this year, put "Less than 1 year."
  • Number of Employees: 1 (This is you).
  • Annual Business Revenue: Enter your projected revenue for the year.
    • Note: It is okay if this is low (e.g., $2,000 or $5,000). Amex primarily approves this based on your personal credit history, which they already know is good.
  • Federal Tax ID (EIN): You do not need one. You can use your Social Security Number (SSN) here.

Step 2: The "Personal Information" Section

  • Total Annual Income: This is your combined income (your day job salary + any freelance income + any other household income you have access to).
    • Why this matters: This is the number they actually care about for your credit limit.

Why this is a safe play for you

  1. Likely No "Hard Pull": Since you already have Amex cards, Amex almost always does a "soft pull" for new card applications. This means it likely won't even ding your credit score to apply.
  2. It separates your expenses: Now you can put every server cost, hardware purchase, and soldering iron on this card. It makes tax season much easier because your freelance expenses are not mixed with your grocery runs.

Next Step: Are you planning to buy anything big for your projects soon? The card usually has a "Welcome Offer" (like 15,000 points after spending $3,000 in 3 months), so you might want to time the application right before a big purchase.

turns.prompt_text: Would it be better to just open up the cards and get the initial bonus of the reward points, and then very very very lowly utilize them only for maybe one or two subscriptions and spread out my subscriptions over many of these cards mainly just getting the initial bonuses?
turns.response_html:
This strategy is not just "better"—it is widely considered the most mathematically profitable way to use credit cards. In the hobby, this is called "Churning" (or "Sign-Up Bonus Hunting").

The math is simple:

  • Daily Spend: Spending $6,000 on a 2% card earns you $120.
  • Bonus Hunting: Spending $6,000 to hit a Sign-Up Bonus (like the Chase Ink) earns you $750+.
  • Result: The bonus strategy is roughly 6x more profitable for the exact same spending.

However, since you mentioned you are "proud" of your current setup and want to do this intelligently, there are three strict rules you must follow to make this work without hurting your credit or getting blacklisted by banks.

Rule 1: The "Sock Drawer" Method (Your Subscription Idea)

Your idea to "spread out subscriptions" is exactly how experts manage this. You can't just get a bonus and never use the card again, or the bank might close it for inactivity.

  • The Strategy: Once you earn the bonus, set up one small automatic monthly charge on the card (like your Audible, MuseScore, or Elevate subscription).
  • The Action: Set the card to "Auto-Pay Full Statement Balance," throw it in a drawer (or a literal sock), and forget it exists.
  • The Benefit: This keeps the account "active" and helps your credit score by increasing your total credit limit while keeping your utilization near 0%.

Rule 2: Watch the "Annual Fee Trap"

This strategy works perfectly for No Annual Fee cards (like the Chase Ink Unlimited or Amex Blue Business Plus). It is dangerous with cards that have fees.

  • The Risk: If you open a card with a $95 fee for the bonus, and then barely use it, you are losing money every year.
  • The Fix: If you get a card with a fee, you must either:
    1. Get enough value from it to justify the fee.
    2. Downgrade it to a "no annual fee" version of that card after Year 1. (Do not cancel it; downgrading keeps the credit history alive).

Rule 3: The Order of Operations (The "Chase Gauntlet")

This is the most critical part for you specifically.

  • Remember the 5/24 Rule? Chase will not let you open their cards if you have opened 5+ personal cards in the last 24 months.
  • If you open random cards first: You will fill up your "slots" with lower-value cards (like a random store card or a small bank card) and permanently block yourself from the high-value Chase bonuses.
  • The Winning Move:
    1. Get the Chase Business cards first (like the Ink Unlimited). Reason: They give you the huge bonus without taking up a "5/24 slot."
    2. Get Chase Personal cards next.
    3. Get Amex/Citi/Other cards last.

Summary: Should you do it?

Yes. If you are organized enough to manage the auto-pays, "Bonus Hunting" will fund your projects far faster than any 2% cash back card ever could.

My recommendation: Start with that Chase Ink Business Unlimited. It gives you the massive bonus ($750 value), has $0 annual fee (so you can "sock drawer" it forever at no cost), and it doesn't hurt your eligibility for future cards.
